entries.title: The best books on Medieval Europe, recommended by Thomas Williams
entries.summary: Europe experienced huge cultural, social and religious change throughout the Middle Ages. You may know it as an age of kings and queens, castles, crusades and chivalric knighthoods, but historians of the period often neglect the seismic events of the far north and east, explains Thomas Williams. Here, he recommends five books that may upend your understanding of medieval Europe. This interview app
entries.content:
Europe experienced huge cultural, social and religious change throughout the Middle Ages. You may know it as an age of kings and queens, castles, crusades and chivalric knighthoods, but historians of the period often neglect the seismic events of the far north and east, explains Thomas Williams. Here, he recommends five books that may upend your understanding of medieval Europe.

Let’s start by defining our terms. When do you consider the medieval period in Europe to have begun, and when did it end?

It’s not a straightforward question, particularly for someone like me, an early medievalist. My idea of the early Middle Ages probably begins somewhat before many other people’s. There’s a popular conception of the Middle Ages as the period from the Norman Conquest onwards: the period of knights, castles, crusades and all the rest of that business.

But for me, if you want to define the medieval period as something in the west of Europe that is post-imperial, but with structured kingship and the institutional presence of the Christian Church, then I think the sixth century is probably the earliest you can reasonably go. But it’s probably not until the seventh century that it starts to look recognisably ‘medieval’.

There is also the complicating factor of what is sometimes called ‘Late Antiquity’, which doesn’t have any hard-and-fast boundaries, but is sometimes imagined to run from the late third to the seventh century.

In terms of the end-point, we’re imprisoned a little bit by Anglophone historiography, which likes to think in terms of the Reformation and Henry VIII’s break with Rome. Obviously, things can feel very different depending on where you’re standing in Europe. But I think the Reformation is still probably the conventional endpoint.

When it comes to my own geographical areas of interest, you could look at something like the collapse of the Teutonic Order in the Baltic, which is broadly speaking part of the Reformation. The secularisation of the Prussian branch of the Teutonic Order occurs in 1525, and that’s an interesting moment. It’s a watershed, where a very distinctive theocratic monastic state, so bound up with ideas and institutions we think of as definitively medieval, breaks down and becomes secularised and Protestant. In Livonia, where the Catholic Order persists, the geopolitics change in the mid-sixteenth century; you suddenly have the Russians under Ivan IV (‘the Terrible’) making land grabs into the Baltic and effectively destroying what remains of the monastic state; it feels like a very different world.

So, yes, this doesn’t nail it down, does it? But very broadly speaking, those would be my parameters. You could pick any number of things, couldn’t you? I suppose the fall of Constantinople to the Turks in 1453 is another contender, but we’re in the right sort of ballpark with the sixteenth century.

I suppose any of these sweeping demarcations have to be, to some extent, artificial. Retrospectively imposing an imaginary framework upon a messy past.

Absolutely. This really gets to the heart of what I’ve been trying to do with my book. It looks at two chapters of medieval history, or what are often seen as distinct chapters: the Viking Age, which in the popular imagination is a time of pagan gods, longships and axe-wielding barbarians, and the age of the Crusades, which is popularly a time of knights, castles, piety and holy war.

They sit very separately, at least from the English perspective, which situates the Norman Conquest right in the middle as a dividing line, with this absurd notion that the Viking Age ended with the death of Harald Hardrada on the battlefield at Stamford Bridge in 1066.

Being familiar with both sides of the divide, it struck me quite forcibly that this is a very false picture, because they bleed into each other in profound ways. The Viking Age doesn’t just stop; it carries on in different forms, with different language and different objectives. But strands and themes carry through deep into the High Middle Ages – longships being one – and things we associate with the High Middle Ages are found in the Viking Age as well: Christian kingship, ideas about holy war, that strange combination of faith and belligerence. So one is in conversation with the other.

Yes. It’s interesting to see how your recommended authors have chosen to organise or bracket their own work. Would you talk through how you made this selection of five books—what you were thinking about?

Well, it was an interesting conundrum. Medieval Europe is a vast subject, spanning an enormous chronological and geographical range. Inevitably, I was looking for books that spoke to my own interests and field of research, but which also said something broader about Europe through that lens.

I knew I couldn’t attempt complete coverage, or I’d be getting into what’s going on in Iberia and the Holy Roman Empire and agricultural change and social transformations and architectural history and goodness knows what else. It would become a fruitless exercise in trying to hit all the bases. So I wanted to find a route that came from a particular perspective. The list reflects my research interests, but also my professional career trajectory and how I’ve arrived at my understanding of Europe.

It was hugely influential because it foregrounded the idea that there is nothing inevitable about Europe as we find it today, or about how it developed in the Middle Ages. Europe was constructed rather than simply coming into being.

In some ways, that feels obvious now, because a lot of work has built on Bartlett’s ideas or challenged them in different ways. But at the time it was published, the notion that Europe was itself a product of colonial expansion, rather than just an exporter of colonial mentalities, was quite radical.

I think that was very persuasive, although parts of it are open to challenge. I would say that Bartlett doesn’t always give due weight to the contingencies around this narrative. The shape of the Europe that emerged was the product of a series of accidents and circumstances that could have turned out differently. Much of the way Europe expanded – north, south, east and west – was also the product of complicated negotiations with other peoples, cultures and ideas, and of the transformations that resulted. It wasn’t entirely a process of erasure and replacement. So there are nuances to the model that I would suggest are valuable to keep in mind. But broadly speaking, it is compelling. Europe was made, it was not inevitable.

Did you meet with this book early in your specialisation?

Not particularly. My background is primarily as an early medievalist, and much of my training was archaeological. I came to the High Middle Ages, and the later Middle Ages, as an extension of previous work I’d done on the Viking Age, which was itself an extension of my work on the even earlier Middle Ages.

I first read this perhaps ten or fifteen years ago, which doesn’t seem that long ago to me. Long enough, I suppose, but it wasn’t formative in my journey, if that’s what you mean. Many of the things it touches on—the Northern Crusades in particular, which form a main plank of his argument about the expansion of Europe’s northeastern frontiers—were subjects I first encountered as an undergraduate.

I had one lecture on the Northern Crusades, and I remember being stunned by it because it was the first time I’d ever encountered this history and I found it mind-blowing. The story of the pagan temple at Arkona and its destruction by the Danes in 1168; the fact that there were still pagans in the Baltic in the late fourteenth century using black powder weapons against the knights of the Teutonic Order; or that Henry Bolingbroke (the future Henry IV) led an army to besiege Vilnius in 1390. This stuff really stayed with me.

I’ve continued to keep abreast of the subject, and writing God’s Hammer was an opportunity to bring a lot of those interests into the book and into conversation with things I’d already studied in more detail. So Bartlett has been in the background for me, but I also find his work interesting because of the broader resonances. He’s talking about the High Middle Ages, but his account of the aggressive manner in which the Roman Church pushed its exclusive message through the conversion period can be applied to the Viking Age and to the seventh-century conversion of the Anglo-Saxons. You can also see it operating within Francia in the sixth century, and you can trace the origins of the process even further back.

Your book God’s Hammer is subtitled ‘A History of the Viking Crusades’. Could you say more about that?

The title is deliberately provocative, because the idea of a Viking ‘crusade’ will feel counterintuitive to most people. There are two things going on here. One is the fact that Scandinavians participated in and led formal crusades, both to the Holy Land and in the Baltic, from the beginning of the twelfth century (towards the end of what would traditionally be seen as the Viking period), into the thirteenth century and beyond.

So there’s that side of the equation: definite Scandinavian involvement in the crusading movement. How ‘Viking’ that was is one question that the book seeks to answer.

The other side of it is that you have what I would call ‘holy wars’ or proto-crusades: aggressive wars of conversion waged by Christian kings long before the First Crusade got underway. You see this very strongly in seventh-century England, in the Frankish world with Clovis and Charlemagne and – most importantly for my book – in Viking Age Scandinavia, where a very aggressive push to Christianise the Scandinavian regions began in the tenth century, bound up with a drive to establish a more dominant model of kingship, a specifically Christian model of kingship.

All of this arguably stretches right back to Constantine at the Milvian Bridge, a foundational narrative for the idea of muscular Christian kingship, wrapped up in Christian symbolism. I’m particularly interested in how those ideas were packaged to appeal to the pagan societies of the north, and what the results of that were.

So I’m coming at this from both ends, which I think is fairly unusual. Not many books have tried to take that long view, and certainly not from a Scandinavian perspective.

Thank you so much. You stay with the Vikings for your next book recommendation, which is Vikings: Life and Legend, a book published in 2014 that offers an overview of the Vikings’ incredible influence.

This is the book associated with the British Museum exhibition in 2014. I joined the project in 2013 as project curator, and – although I can’t claim credit for the intellectual formation of the exhibition; the book had already been written by the time I joined the team – I laid a lot of the groundwork for the show, working with the objects, writing text for the exhibition itself and developing and delivering the public programme.

The bigger argument the exhibition was making was that we shouldn’t see the Vikings as an isolated phenomenon affecting Britain and parts of western Europe: a walk-on part in history, or a disruptive event that arrived like a spell of bad weather. In truth the Viking world had an enormous footprint. Through their maritime culture, the Vikings became the first people to reach four continents. They forged communication networks and effected cultural transformations that had a profound impact on the trajectory of Europe. They shaped the political destiny of multiple European nations: England, Scotland, Ireland, France, Russia and Ukraine among them. The exhibition was giving the Vikings back some of their dignity, agency and transformative power in the European story.

That’s hugely important for how we understand the medieval world as an interconnected whole, rather than a collection of isolated national stories.

This is an interesting one. It doesn’t specifically address the medieval world as it was, but rather how our idea of it—and, specifically, of the Vikings—is largely a product of the nineteenth century. It’s a creation of Victorian scholarship, even down to the popularisation of ‘Viking’ as the term for these people. Before the Victorians, they had been called ‘Danes’ or ‘heathens’, and sometimes Norsemen. There was no fixed way of describing them, and then ‘Viking’ emerged as a preferred term in that period, for better or worse.

The ‘Vikings’ were a Victorian creation, and the implications are huge, because the Victorians also brought assumptions about race, heredity, empire and the superiority of the Germanic world. Those assumptions had implications for how Britain saw itself and how its role as a Christian empire was perceived.

There’s a massive amount of baggage bound up with the creation and perpetuation of these ideas. Again, it gets me into this business of not wanting to accept the categories and boundaries established through historiographical convention.

This has implications for the whole medieval period and for medieval Europe as an entity: what defines Europe, what defines Christianity, what defines paganism, and so on. When you start to peel back the layers of the onion, you can quite swiftly find that you’re looking at a nineteenth-century antiquarian construction founded on little more than late-imperial prejudices about the world in which its creators lived.

It’s a very useful prompt for readers, to remind them to think critically about perceived wisdom. I’ll keep us moving: next we have Christian Raffensperger’s Reimagining Europe: Kievan Rus’ in the Medieval World. This is a topic I’m not familiar with at all—could you introduce me?

Yes. This is helpful I think because it sits in a useful conversation with Bartlett’s book. It’s not a direct corrective, but a complicating factor. What Raffensperger is essentially saying is that we tend to look at Europe as a western-European-centric entity that expands into a sort of ‘outland’: the amorphous world beyond Frankish Latin Christendom.

Raffensperger argues that, if you look at it from an Eastern European perspective, you find yourself in a highly developed, sophisticated Greek-Christian world, both in Byzantium and in Kyivan Rūs – the precursor state, if you like, to modern Russia, Belarus and Ukraine.

His core argument is that if you strip away preconceived notions of what Europe is, you find that Rūs, as it was then constituted, had much deeper connections with western Europe and was more important in terms of its diplomatic, economic and outward-facing connections than we tend to assume. It should really be thought of as a Christian European power, no different from medieval France, the Holy Roman Empire or England. It’s an attempt to reframe what we mean by Europe.

If you think about Bartlett’s argument, his perspective is of a western Frankish Christendom that is expanding outwards towards the east. Well, yes, it is, but it is meeting something equally sophisticated, equally Christian and equally vibrant. It’s only historical accident, in the shape of the Mongol invasions, that really scrambles that map. We don’t know what Europe would look like had it not been for the disruption of southern routes to the Black Sea in the thirteenth century, or for that matter the sack of Constantinople by the Crusaders in 1204. These were historical moments with huge transformative effects. We don’t have a counterfactual for what Europe might otherwise have become.

What’s coming through in your book recommendations is an invigorating sense of destabilisation. They call into question everything we think of when we think of medieval Europe, right?

Yes, I like that! I think that’s one of the reasons I’ve been drawn to these writers and books. As God’s Hammer probably implies, I’m interested in the collision of worlds: what happens in those interactions, what are the messy crossovers, and where are the moments of contingency on which so much of this history hangs. Are we looking at things clearly? Are we standing far enough away to get the proper picture? Or are we enmeshed in modern, preconceived visions? All these books address that in different ways.

This is the newest book on the list. It only came out this year, and it’s a wonderful book. It sets out in clear and logical detail a subject that is woefully undertaught, misunderstood and, frankly, not even known about by many: despite the fact that these crusades fundamentally transformed the boundaries of Europe in ways that other crusading movements spectacularly failed to accomplish.

A lot of people studying medieval history would be astounded to learn that Scottish crusaders travelled to fight holy wars in the frozen forests of Lithuania, or that the biggest castle in Europe – Malbork in Poland – was built as the headquarters of the Teutonic Order in former East Prussia. These are bonkers narratives if you’ve never encountered them before. The landscape and climate give the whole thing an amazing cinematic quality, with its wilderness and snow. It’s quite a wonderful story.

Crucially, Pluskowski’s book fundamentally updates the previous history of the subject, Eric Christiansen’s The Northern Crusades, published in 1997. That’s also a great book and one that had a great influence on me personally. But it’s also nearly thirty years old, and there has been a huge amount of archaeological work on the northern Crusades that has been conducted in the last fifteen or twenty years, much of it led by Aleksander himself.

I actually dug with him for a season in eastern Poland, in Masuria. His work produced a massive amount of environmental data that show how the Crusades transformed the physical landscape, patterns of land-use and biodiversity in the region, as well as the physical castles and churches built by the Teutonic Knights and others during their conquests, and the cultural and religious changes experienced by people in material terms. The Black Cross draws on all of this new work as well as the medieval chronicles of the period to really enrich understanding of the period. So a big thumbs-up for that.

Thank you, and it’s great to have a sense of spread in the book choices—we have books from several decades ago coming right up into the present. As a closing question, do you have any other suggestions to offer readers seeking to expand their understanding of the medieval world?

I’d emphasise a couple of things I’ve already mentioned. Any approach to the Middle Ages risks getting bogged down in older scholarship that brings a lot of inherited baggage with it. People should be alert to that: always challenge the assumption on the page.

The other thing I’d say, if people are really interested in this stuff, is to go back to the primary sources. It’s all very well reading a secondary work that retells a historical narrative, but you’re effectively reading another layer of interpretation, which colours the framing of the history it’s trying to tell. If you go to the primary record, you can see what the chronicler was actually trying to say in their own words. Of course, we’re often dealing with translations, so it’s not completely straightforward. But it’s one of the easiest ways to cut through a lot of that accumulated historiographical or cultural baggage.

It’s particularly important at the moment because the Middle Ages is where a lot of ethnonationalist narratives draw their sustenance. If those narratives aren’t challenged, or if people aren’t looking at the actual sources on which they’re supposedly based, they’re going to be easily misled. It happens all the time.

Thomas Williams is a historian and archaeologist and the author of Viking Britain, Viking London and Lost Realms. He was project curator of the British Museum’s major international exhibition Vikings: Life and Legend(2014), and later curated the museum's early medieval coin collection. He holds a PhD from UCL and is a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries and Royal Historical Society. His new book God's Hammer: a History of the Viking Crusades is out now.

entries.title: New in Ancient History
entries.summary: We love books about ancient history at Five Books. Not only is it relaxing to escape from the present by reading about events several millennia ago, but the brutality of that period also helps put our modern challenges in perspective. One exciting trend in the past few years is a move away from accounts of ancient Rome and Greece to other ancient civilisations. Here's a roundup of some of the book
entries.content:
We love books about ancient history at Five Books. Not only is it relaxing to escape from the present by reading about events several millennia ago, but the brutality of that period also helps put our modern challenges in perspective. One exciting trend in the past few years is a move away from accounts of ancient Rome and Greece to other ancient civilisations. Here's a roundup of some of the books published recently.

A really immersive book that makes it hard not to pack your bags and head to Tunisia is Carthage: A New History of an Ancient Empire by Eve MacDonald, a classicist and archaeologist who teaches at Cardiff University:

The Library of Ancient Wisdom, a book by Assyriologist Selena Wisnom, takes us to Iraq in the 7th century BCE and the library of Ashurbanipal. It’s been shortlisted for the Wolfson Prize, the UK’s most prestigious history prize:

Staying in Mesopotamia, our contributing editor Tuva Kahrs also really enjoyed Between Two Rivers and the way it’s concerned with people’s lives. “I particularly loved the description of bricks with dog paw prints and clay writing tablets with children’s fingerprints from thousands of years ago,” she writes. She interviewed the author, Moudhy Al-Rashid, on the best books about Mesopotamia.

We spoke to historian Lloyd Llewellyn-Jones about the Persian Empire a few years ago. He’s now written a book on Babylon, ‘the mother of all cities.’ Given how it’s been vilified in the Biblical tradition, it’s quite fun to read a book that puts the record straight. “The Babylon you will meet in this book was a thriving, rich and advanced ancient Near Eastern city with a singular identity, which it maintained for well over 2000 years,” he writes.

We’re fans of books by Robert Harris at Five Books, as his historical fiction tends to be based on primary sources, and it’s a relaxing way to learn about history. Agrippa is about Augustus’s best friend and presents him as the genius behind the military victories that enabled Octavian, the great-nephew of Julius Caesar, to become the first Roman emperor.

Also recently recommended on Five Books in historical fiction is Boudicca’s Daughter by Elodie Harper. Set in Britain at the time of the Roman invasion, it’s about the daughter of the late Iron Age queen, Boudicca. According to Alex Bescoby, one of the judges of the Wilbur Smith Adventure Writing Prize, the book is realistic, in as much as it can be “about a culture that was essentially eradicated and happened a very long time ago. There’s not a lot to work from, but I found the story compelling.” (We also have nonfiction book recommendations about Boudicca, by Richard Hingley, a professor of Archaeology at Durham University).

October 25, 2026

Five Books aims to keep its book recommendations and interviews up to date. If you are the interviewee and would like to update your choice of books (or even just what you say about them) please email us at [email protected]

entries.title: The Best Shakespeare Comedies, recommended by Heather Hirschfeld
entries.summary: For Shakespeare, comedy was not simply about laughter, but about conflict and confusion giving way to resolution and a happy ending — at least by the standards of the Elizabethan era. The dilemmas these plays explore are still strikingly relevant, argues Heather Hirschfeld. She explores five Shakespearean comedies that speak to us today — on everything from power to identity to shared humanity, al
entries.content:
What defines or characterises a comedy in this context?

I can’t help but think about Shakespeare’s own suspicion of genre categories. I will quote Hamlet for you, because for me everything gets oriented around that play. A troupe of players is coming to Elsinore, and Polonius praises them as “The best actors in the world, either for tragedy, comedy, history, pastoral, pastoral-comical, historical-pastoral, tragical-historical, tragical-comical-historical-pastoral, scene individable, or poem unlimited” – Shakespeare is aware of and having a gentle laugh at our commitment to dramatic categories.

But genre definitions are important. Generic expectations both orient us and allow us to be surprised. Shakespeare and his contemporaries inherited a definition that comedy was “the imitation of life, the glass of custom, and the image of truth.” They also knew the Aristotelian distinction between comedy and tragedy, which traffics in figures who are greater or more admirable than we are. Comedies focus on characters closer to our own station, who are absorbed in the activities of daily life, and who face obstacles that block their practical goals or romantic desires. So a compact definition of comedy is drama that sets its characters in difficult situations, runs them through various dilemmas and complications, and resolves those complications in ways that afford new possibilities for family, community, and belonging.

Could we say something about the categories in the 1623 collection of his plays, the First Folio?

Yes. The title page of the Folio reads: ‘Master William Shakespeare’s comedies, histories, and tragedies’. Shakespeare’s fellows and compilers are also committed to generic distinctions. The first play in the Folio is The Tempest, which is today considered a romance rather than a comedy. In the Oxford Handbook of Shakespearean Comedy, I explain why we now label The Tempest, The Winter’s Tale and Cymbeline in this way. But it’s worth reminding your readers that they were grouped in the comedies in Shakespeare’s time, although we’ve plucked them apart.

It’s almost cruel to ask a Shakespeare scholar to pick the best five of any kind of Shakespeare play. What criteria have you used to pick your plays today?

It was indeed painful. To make it easier, I used the concept of “best for”: I asked myself what plays I enjoy most, and what I think other readers and viewers would enjoy most – but then added the qualifier, “best for doing X”. In this way, I made explicit what audiences often do with Shakespeare: make his works and language serve different purposes. I’m always very conscious of Shakespeare’s line in The Merchant of Venice, “the devil can cite scripture for his purpose.” As our “secular scripture,” Shakespeare is available for different uses.

Great, let’s talk about your first choice. What is The Comedy of Errors best for?

This is best for starting a semester with an undergraduate class. I’m a professor at the University of Tennessee, and I teach a wide range of classes. One of my favourites to teach is an introduction to Shakespeare. Students in this course are usually not English majors, but they need an arts and humanities credit or a writing concentration class for their general education requirements.

I love this play as a starting point for students. It itself is an early play, a “beginning” for Shakespeare. It has a seemingly tidy structure – it obeys Aristotelian unities of time and place – but it opens up into a chaotic world of errors – wanderings, mistakes, misapprehensions of self and other. It’s one of Shakespeare’s shortest plays, but it contains in little all the concerns he takes up with more consistency in later comedies and tragedies.

Great. Tell us about the story.

It’s a plot of mistaken identity. Two sets of twins inhabit the city of Ephesus, but they don’t know that the other set is there. That’s the source of much of the laughter, as the audience knows that the twins were separated some twenty-five years earlier, and that one set has been sailing across the Mediterranean in search of the other set. The situation becomes a rich ground for Shakespeare to dramatize family relationships (particularly relevant for a play whose setting is the same as Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians): between husband and wife, parent and child, and sibling and sibling. The relationships play out against a background of global commerce, as Ephesus is an active port city, and it’s in a trade war with Syracuse, the home of one of the sets of twins. My students are very alert to the idea that the play is about, among other things, migration and immigration.

Shakespeare took the basic plot from Plautus’s Menaechmi, a classical Latin play, and he enriched it by doubling the sets of twins – in Plautus there’s only one set, a merchant and the sibling searching for him. Shakespeare gives each twin, both named Antipholus – I know, it’s very confusing – a companion named Dromio, who is really their servant or slave. The addition of the Dromios puts new emphasis on the unsettling dynamics between masters and servants. Shakespeare also extends the story of husband and wife that he gets from Plautus, paying special attention to Antipholus of Ephesus’s wife, Adriana, and her fears and jealousies. My students – and surely audiences generally – are always taken with the plight of Adriana, who is so preoccupied by the possibility that her husband is cheating that she mistakes his twin for him. Shakespeare also frames the story of the Antipholi twins with that of their father, Egeon, who, as a Syracusan, has been imprisoned in Ephesus and faces execution.

The play is tied to the sea. We learn in the play’s first act that the sets of twins, along with Egeon and his wife, were separated by a shipwreck, and all the characters are concerned with setting sail, whether to escape Ephesus or to continue their trading ventures. So the language is infused by a maritime sensibility, and its most striking metaphors are spoken by characters who compare themselves to water drops.

This is the earliest play on your list. In the introduction to your Handbook, you mention that it will refute the developmental model, that the plays go from more joyful to more ironic over time… Is this a joyful play?

Yes, I think that’s a fair assessment. The endings of Shakespeare’s comedies are always complicated, with festivity and joy punctuated with melancholy or uncertainty. Comedy of Errors is almost entirely celebratory: after all the farcical mishaps of the first four acts, the twins are reunited with their siblings, Egeon is reunited with his long-lost wife, Antipholus of Syracuse gains a wife, the sister of Adriana, and Adriana and Antipholus of Ephesus at least seem reconciled. We know realistically that the happy ending cannot compensate for the many years the families have been separated, nor can it undo the beatings we have seen the Dromios sustain, but we can participate in the fantasy resolution and the way the play, in the language of Ephesians, has “redeemed the time.”

What I refer to in the Handbook is the finding of many of my contributors: that all Shakespeare’s comedies are vulnerable to a tragic turn. This potential inheres in the language and depends on performance. Taming of the Shrew is not on my list, but that’s an early play in which the ending – when Katherine seems to submit to her husband – can be performed in a number of ways. It can be played as though her deference to her husband is a sign that she has been entirely broken by him, or it can be played as though she is slyly mimicking what he’d like her to say. Or the actors can perform the conclusion with a shared aplomb, so that Katherine and Petruchio seem to be collaborating in a joke. So much depends on performance.

Let’s look at your second choice now: Measure for Measure – which is debatable, but listed as a comedy in the Folio…

I would put Measure and Merchant together under the heading of ‘problem plays.’ The term ‘problem play’ does not come up in the Hamlet list. It’s a modern invention. But it does name what you were gesturing to before – their endings feel far from resolved, and they leave us in the uncomfortable position of watching characters who remain alienated, outside the communal circle, on the edge of a tragedy. In Measure, the focus of the ending is on Isabella, who starts the play hoping to become a nun. She is forced to leave the convent and, at the end of the play, receives silently what seems like an inescapable marriage proposal from a man who has deceived her. I’ve seen one performance in which this whole experience absolutely shatters her. It’s easy even just reading the play to note the painful ending, but to see her silence at the end performed as traumatic brokenness feels very different.

In the Folio of 1623, Measure is listed as a comedy, and it is a comedy in form — it begins with a complicated political and domestic situation which it resolves by bringing multiple couples together. But its substance is dark; it feels much more driven by the spectre of death than the promise of pleasure.

Interesting. What’s it best for?

It’s best for talking about what the play calls the “properties of government”: the relationship of the state to its subjects, the shapes that tyranny takes, and the role of sexuality in contemporary politics and religion. Its combination of politics, sex and religion – really its combination of political and sexual abuse — is so pertinent for our own moment, as it was for Shakespeare’s. The play interrogates what it means to be in a position of power and to be a subject of that power.

Tell us a little about the plot.

Duke Vincentio is Duke of Vienna, and he’s worried that his city has become disorderly and unruly, and he blames himself for being too lax in enforcing the laws. His way of solving this problem is to pretend to leave Vienna and to place his deputy, Angelo, in charge, as a kind of “bad cop.” Vincentio dons the disguise of a friar, so he can hide behind the scenes and observe what happens to his city in his absence. He thus witnesses the licence not only of his citizens but also of the seemingly puritanical Angelo.

Angelo, in his effort to instil order, wants to execute Claudio, Isabella’s brother, for fornication (sex outside of marriage). When Isabella, having left the convent, pleads to Angelo on Claudio’s behalf, Angelo makes an indecent proposal: if Isabella will sleep with him, he’ll free her brother.  The proposal makes crystal clear that chastity, the condition of a patriarchal sexual and political economy, inflames the desire of a seemingly chaste man. So that’s the set up.

It certainly seems set for tragedy.

And I haven’t even gotten into the news we learn later that Angelo has abandoned a former lover when she lost her dowry. And that Duke Vincentio knew about this. But as it’s a comedy, we’ve got to rescue everybody from Angelo’s obscene demand.

The play becomes even more problematic when Isabella goes to her brother to tell him what has happened, expecting that he will be willing to die rather than she be forced to have sex with Angelo. But when he does imply that he wants her to do that, she is outraged to the point that she promises to “pray a thousand prayers for thy death.” Her response is another element of the problem play: the postulant turns on her brother with the same viciousness and the same literal-mindedness that the false deputy Angelo uses against her.

Your third choice we’ve already touched on as a good partner for Measure. Tell us about The Merchant of Venice.

Yes. This play too is relevant to our contemporary moment, addressing religious and racial difference. Religion and race are intimately associated in Shakespeare’s time, as both are understood to inhere in the blood as well as the skin.

I can quickly remind folks that Antonio is the merchant of the title, not Shylock, the Jew and best-known character. Antonio is a Christian merchant, and he agrees to take on the burden of a loan on behalf of his friend Bassanio, whom he secretly adores – it’s a relationship that various scholars have seen as either explicitly or implicitly homoerotic. The loan will enable Bassanio to woo Portia, and Antonio agrees to a bond with Shylock for 3,000 ducats. The bond stipulates that if Antonio cannot pay his debt, Shylock is entitled to “a pound of your fair flesh” (the scholar Ian Smith has paid attention to “fairness” as a signal of racial and religious difference here).

Antonio can’t repay the debt on time. Shylock, furious at the fact that his daughter has eloped with a Christian, demands his pound of flesh. The case comes to trial in front of the cross-dressed Portia, Bassanio’s beloved, who is disguised as a judge. She asks Shylock to be merciful, but when he refuses to give up the bond, she awards him his pound of flesh. Just as Shylock approaches Antonio, however, she warns him not to spill any blood and not to take “a jot” more than a single pound. Which is impossible to do, so the tables are turned on Shylock. He’s accused of threatening the life of a Christian and Portia rules that he must convert and relinquish his possessions.

A mixed ending indeed…

You can hear the devastating anti-Jewish tropes operating here. Shylock is presented as the bloodthirsty villain who wants to kill the martyr-like Antonio.

But at the same time as it traffics in these anti-Jewish tropes, the play also gives space and language to Shylock’s suffering and humanity. “Hath not a Jew eyes?” he asks, a question that seems directed not only to the other characters but to the audience. The play walks a tightrope between the particularism associated with the Jew, and the universalist claims of the Christian. Nobody talks about this better than Janet Adelman in a book called Blood Relations, which addresses the Christian characters’ own sense of their inheritance from a Jewish tradition, and their need to reject and separate from it.

At the same time, the figure of the Jew can be seen to stand in for a number of other outsiders. In Protestant England, for instance, Catholics were compared to Jews.  Emma Smith suggests that Shylock can be read as a stand-in for economic and religious migrants in London. From this perspective, Shylock’s plea makes the play “best for” acknowledging claims to a shared humanity. I think Shakespeare has captured something about a uniquely Jewish experience of historic marginalization in this play. But it’s important, particularly in this moment when anti-Semitism has been so weaponized, to extend Shylock’s powerful claim to the voices of other groups or peoples. I say this as somebody who is Jewish.

This brings us to The Oxford Handbook of Shakespearean Comedy, where all the essays are framed around the theme of ‘encounter’. I can see now how fertile that would be. We’ve talked about sexual and gendered encounters, racial and religious encounters… Did the theme come first and shape the essays, or vice versa?

It felt to me like we needed to have some organising principle for the volume, especially because the editors did not want individual chapters on each play. That really put pressure on me to think of ways to bring plays together in units of two or three or even four. I have to give tonnes of credit to my contributors who did that synthesizing work under the broad banner of an encounter in extraordinary ways. One example that I was especially surprised by is by John Parker, who put together Comedy of Errors, Merchant of Venice and The Merry Wives of Windsor under the heading of “holy adultery.” And Catherine Richardson did wonderful work on domestic encounters in her chapter.

‘Encounter’ also allowed me to get at a major concern of contemporary scholarship: the ways in which Shakespeare’s plays embrace the globe. And I mean the globe of geography and cosmography, although we should mention the Globe Theatre too. The language of ‘encounter’ speaks to early modern exploration and international contact, and using it allowed the volume to thematize the ways Shakespeare’s comedies travel across such a wide swath of the world. It’s worth just re-listing the locales of the comedies I’ve discussed: Vienna, Venice, Ephesus…

Also, as somebody invested in psychoanalysis, I relied on the idea of encounter as a prompt to focus on intimate relationships. So, as much as the theme gave contributors purchase on global Shakespeare, it also enabled us to talk about the one-to-one interactions in the plays.

Well, that brings us very nicely to your next choice, which certainly features some beloved one-to-one encounters: what is Much Ado About Nothing best for?

This is best for navigating the thin line between war and sex or violence and love.

A group of soldiers return from war to Messina, Sicily.  The backdrop of armed battle sets up a battle of the sexes. The best known– or as you say, beloved — of these battles is between the characters Beatrice and Benedick, the model couple of witty romantic banter. But there are other battles of the sexes. Claudio falls in love with Hero, but allows his leader, Don Pedro, to woo her on his behalf. We thus see a kind of “battle” develop between Claudio and Hero but also between Claudio and Don Pedro over Hero. The villainous Don John exploits this situation, convincing Claudio that Hero has been unfaithful so that he rejects her at the altar. The characters get fooled by the very traps they set in order to pursue their love objects. And the women bear the burden of the traps. The triumph of the play is that Benedick gives up his masculine ties to defend Hero and Beatrice.

Much Ado marks the height of Shakespeare’s work with the clown Will Kemp, who plays the linguistically challenged constable Dogberry (he’s always using words incorrectly). Dogberry and his comrades discover that Don John has manufactured the claim against Hero. As his partner-in-crime Borachio notes, “What your wisdoms could not discover, these shallow fools have brought to light.” That is the source of comic delight: the lowly Dogberry sees, despite himself, through the masquerades and plots of the high-born courtiers.

The clown raises an interesting point – we haven’t touched on the more standard modern meaning of a comedy: something funny. Will we still be laughing at these plays?

That is a great question. I should hope so. Good performances bring to life the plays’ rich range of puns, jokes, and farcical scenes. And the tension that we have been discussing, between the serious and the humorous, only heightens the moments of release and laughter.

In the Handbook, Jeremy Lopez’s ‘Imagining Shakespeare’s Audience’ historicizes comedy by suggesting how certain characters – often in smaller parts – help direct the audience to laugh, as if they were teaching playgoers to recognize what is funny.

I do think that Shakespeare’s comedies, both then and now, insist that we stay alert to what makes us laugh, and to the possibility that we laugh at the expense of another person. Shakespeare does this by constructing inset plays, so that the off-stage audience can watch the on-stage audience as a kind of mirror for what they’re doing in the moment. That might take us on to Twelfth Night and the duping of Malvolio…

Your fifth choice. Tell us about Twelfth Night, and then we’ll come back to this question of comedy.

This is another shipwreck play and another twin play, so we are coming full circle with Comedy of Errors. It’s best for studying the shapes of human desire. I’ll give you a quick synopsis…

The shipwrecked comic heroine Viola puts on the disguise of a page boy named Cesario to serve Orsino, the Count of Illyria. Viola is of course played, like all other female characters in Shakespeare’s time, by a boy actor, so there’s a layering or implicating of gender identities from the second scene. Viola – at once she, he, they – ends up in a love triangle. Orsino sends Viola/Cesario to woo Olivia on his behalf; Olivia falls in love with Viola, whom she thinks is Cesario; and Viola/Cesario is in love with Orsino. This triangle is matched by another one, with a homoerotic twist: Antonio adores Sebastian, Viola’s supposedly lost twin brother, while Olivia and Sebastian pair off.

These triangles seem conventional now, but they completely destabilise these characters’ worlds. Willingly or unwillingly, they inhabit different ‘subject positions’ – different ways of perceiving and responding to the world than they are used to. For our own times, the play speaks to the fluidity and fragility of sexual and gender orientations.

I want to call attention to a line that Viola/Cesario offers: she’s distressed at the effects of her disguise, and she says, “Disguise, I see thou art a wickedness.” Here she’s echoing the language of anti-theatricalists – those critics of the theatre in Shakespeare’s time who were concerned about it in the same way that people now are concerned when they don’t like video games. They maintained that if you see a play, you’re going to act like what you see. So she’s a pre-modern critic of acting, and yet she continues to perform; and it’s by performing that she becomes increasingly self-aware. I think that’s one of the things we appreciate in her playing both Viola and Cesario at the same time, and inhabiting these different identities.

Another very relevant play. And it links back to the question of our implication in the comedy?

Twelfth Night is so meta-dramatic – it calls attention to itself as a work of theatre by creating internal plays. Mariah and Sir Toby trick the character Malvolio, Olivia’s steward, to get back at him for aspiring above his class position in a condescending way. They plot to convince Malvolio that Olivia is in love with him, and they use his response to humiliate him. Their “play” is a joke on, but also a punishment of, Malvolio. In fact, there’s a great line where Sir Toby says, “Come, we’ll have him in a dark room and bound… We may carry it thus, for our pleasure and his penance”. So we learn here that our laughter and delight, like Toby and Mariah’s, is often at the cost of somebody else – he’s being punished while we’re taking pleasure in it.

We delight in these plays. We should delight in them. They are meant to give us access to shared experiences. But I do think there’s a little voice behind the scenes that’s saying, just know that you’re complicit in this.

The self-recognition in comedy is so important. If tragedy is leading you to a catharsis, the purging of pity and fear – if you go back to the Aristotelian definitions – then comedy should make you aware of what you’re laughing at. Or, in my Handbook’s terms, aware of your encounters.
